title: Dropping Color: The Greyscale Pattern Lab
excerpt: Every week so far lands on the same weak spot: models read these puzzles' shapes almost perfectly but read their colors only partially. If color is the bottleneck, the fix is probably in how the puzzle is drawn — so this week we built a tool to design and preview color-free representations: greyscale shades, hand-drawn glyphs, or uploaded icons for each value 0–9.

sections.heading: In Plain Terms
sections.body: Weeks 3–6 kept finding the same thing: an AI can look at one of these colored-grid puzzles and copy its shape back almost perfectly, but it gets a lot of the colors wrong. So the natural question is: what if we stop relying on color? Instead of ten colors, what if each value were a distinct grey shade, or a little drawn symbol? This week's tool lets you invent those visuals by hand, drop in a real puzzle, and immediately see the whole thing redrawn with your design — so you can judge which representation reads clearest and best preserves the puzzle before we ever spend model time on it.

sections.heading: Why Now
sections.body: The Week 4 legend win and the Week 5–6 cross-model results told a consistent story: swapping models doesn't fix the color problem — the bottleneck is how the puzzle is drawn, not which model reads it. Adding a color legend already lifted accuracy once; the obvious next lever is the encoding itself. Before running a formal experiment we need a fast way to iterate on the encoding and eyeball it on real puzzles: does a greyscale ramp stay legible? Do hand-drawn glyphs read more distinctly than shades? Does the puzzle's structure survive the swap?

sections.heading: What We Built
sections.body:
A single self-contained HTML page — the Greyscale Pattern Lab — that runs entirely in the browser with no dependencies and no server, and it is hosted on this site so anyone can use it directly. You design a per-value visual for each of 0–9, load an ARC-style puzzle JSON, and every train/test grid is re-rendered with your design; export the result as PNG to compare encodings. Highlights:
  • Three render modes — grey shades (a tunable grey ramp), custom images (your uploaded or hand-drawn glyph per value), and original colors (the standard ARC palette, as a side-by-side baseline).
  • Draw or upload — an in-browser drawing canvas with an adjustable brush and a grey-shade slider for designing greyscale glyphs, or upload an image for any value; value 0 defaults to a plain background but is editable.
  • Tunable — grey-ramp dark/light ends and invert, background, cell size, gridlines, and an optional digit-label overlay.
  • Portable — paste or upload puzzle JSON, export the rendered puzzle as PNG, and your designs persist in the browser between sessions. Light/dark theme matches the rest of the site.

Open the Greyscale Pattern Lab →  ·  Read the full Week 7 report →

sections.heading: How to Use It
items: Open the Greyscale Pattern Lab and click Load sample to render a puzzle immediately.
For each value, click Draw to sketch a glyph or Upload an image — or stay in Grey shades mode and tune the ramp.
Switch between Grey shades, Custom images, and Original colors to compare how each encoding reads on the same puzzle.
Paste your own puzzle JSON (standard train/test format) or upload a .json file, then Render.
Export PNG to save an encoding for comparison or to drop into a future report.

sections.heading: Next Steps
sections.body: With a design bench in hand, the plan is to pick the greyscale/glyph encoding that reads most clearly, render the puzzle set with it, and run it back through the Week 6 baseline tool — testing directly whether a color-free representation closes the perception gap that every model has shown so far.

title: Can They Actually Solve? A Three-Way Model Baseline Tool
excerpt: So far we've only measured whether a vision model can copy a puzzle back as data. That's perception, not problem-solving. This week we built an interactive tool that separates the two — measuring, per model, whether it can solve a puzzle blind, reconstruct it, and solve it from its own reconstruction.

sections.heading: In Plain Terms
sections.body: Everything up to now has asked one question: can an AI look at a picture of a colored-grid puzzle and faithfully copy it back as data? That's about seeing. But the puzzles are meant to be solved — you study a few before/after examples and figure out the rule, then apply it to a new grid. This week we're building a small self-contained web tool that measures three different things for any model: (1) can it solve the puzzle cold, straight from the image; (2) can it copy the puzzle back as data (what we've measured before); and (3) if we make it copy the puzzle first and then solve from its own copy, does that help or hurt? Line those three up and we get a clean baseline of what today's models can actually do — and a reusable instrument for testing why.

sections.heading: Why Now
sections.body: Weeks 3–5 established one robust fact: current vision models read MARC puzzle structure perfectly but read colors only partially (~50–80%), across model families. Every one of those numbers is a perception score — how faithfully the model reconstructs what it sees. We have never measured whether any model can solve a puzzle at all. Before going further, we want to cleanly separate two things that reconstruction scoring tangles together: can the model see the grid, and can the model reason to the answer? A model could see perfectly and still fail to solve, or mis-see yet still infer the rule. The only way to know is to measure solving and perception independently, then measure what happens when you chain them.

sections.heading: The Three Measurements
items: Blind solve — hand the model only the puzzle image (train pairs visible, test answer hidden) and ask it to produce the test output grid directly. No reconstruction step. Scored against the known answer.

Reconstruction — ask the model to copy the visible puzzle back as JSON. Scored on cell fidelity over what it can actually see (train grids + test input), exactly the perception metric from prior weeks.

Reconstruct-then-solve — a two-step chain: first the model reconstructs the image to JSON, then it solves the puzzle from its own reconstructed JSON (text only, no image). This exposes how perception errors propagate into solving.

sections.heading: What We Built
sections.body:
A single self-contained HTML page — the Model Baseline Analysis tool — that runs entirely in the browser against MindRouter, no server or build step. It renders the puzzle to an image client-side (same ARC palette, legend, and hidden-test-output “?” as our Python pipeline), so the model sees exactly what prior weeks fed it. Highlights:
  • Live model picker — the dropdown is populated from GET /v1/models on the cluster, so you always choose from what's actually available; you can also type a custom id.
  • Streaming requests — server-sent events with the per-model shaping we settled on in Week 4 (thinking flag only for Qwen, JSON-object mode otherwise, no-retry on 404).
  • Two-sided scoring — solving is graded by exact match (whole answer grid, the ARC standard) and per-cell accuracy; reconstruction is graded on visible cells only (train grids + test input), cleanly separating perception from solving.
  • Visual diffs — the model's grids sit side-by-side with the truth, wrong cells outlined in red, reasoning traces and raw responses tucked into expandable panels.
  • Portable logs — every run is saved in-browser and can be downloaded as a JSON log and reloaded later to review, so results don't live only on one machine.

Read the full Week 6 report →  ·  the tool itself runs locally (code/tools/model-baseline-analysis.html) — it needs the CORS proxy and an API key, so it isn't hosted on this site.

sections.heading: How to Use It
items: Start the local proxy once — uv run code/scripts/cors_proxy.py. Browsers can't call MindRouter directly (no CORS header), so this tiny stdlib proxy forwards requests and adds the header; it also injects your key from keys.txt, so the API-key field can stay blank.
Open the tool locally — code/tools/model-baseline-analysis.html — the base URL defaults to the proxy at http://localhost:8811/v1 and is remembered in your browser.
Click Refresh models and pick a model; toggle thinking mode if you want it (Qwen-only, off by default).
Choose a puzzle JSON file from code/puzzles/; the rendered image preview shows exactly what the model will see.
Press Run all three — blind solve, reconstruct, and reconstruct-then-solve run in sequence and the scored results appear as a card.
Download the log to keep results, or Load a previous log to review past runs — logs are portable JSON, so results don't live only on one machine.

sections.heading: Scope
sections.body: To be clear about what this is not: we are not yet starting the core MARC research question (does the metaphor clue help models solve?). This week is about building the measuring instrument and getting a definitive capability baseline — solve, reconstruct, and reconstruct-then-solve — so every later experiment has a clean reference point.

title: Is It Just Qwen? Testing the Color Bottleneck Across Models
excerpt: Weeks 3–4 found one vision model reads MARC structure perfectly but misreads colors. This week we tried the same task on three more models — including one from a different maker — to see if that's a fluke. It isn't: every model gets the shape right and the colors only partly right.

sections.heading: In Plain Terms
sections.body: We're testing whether AI "vision" models can look at a picture of a small colored-grid puzzle and faithfully copy it back as data — the right shape and the right colors. Last week, one model copied the shape perfectly but got only about two-thirds of the colors right. The worry: maybe that one model is just bad at color. So this week we handed the same puzzles to three more models, including one built by a different company. They all did the same thing — shapes correct, colors only partly right. In short: reading color from these images is a shared weak spot across today's models, not a flaw in any single one. That tells us the fix is to make the pictures easier to read, not just to swap in a different model.

sections.heading: Why This Week
sections.body: Every conclusion so far rested on a single model, qwen/qwen3.6-35b: it reconstructs MARC puzzle structure flawlessly but reads colors only about half to two-thirds of the time, and naive chain-of-thought doesn't lift that. Before building further, the obvious risk to rule out is that those findings are an artifact of one model. So this week ran the exact same image→JSON reconstruction task across other vision-capable vLLM models on MindRouter.

sections.heading: Methodology
items: Ran the identical image-only reconstruction task (no JSON source) on three additional vision models: google/gemma-4-31b (a different model family), qwen/qwen3.5-122b, and qwen3-vl:32b
Preliminary scale: a 3-puzzle subset — enough to see whether the qualitative pattern reappears, not yet a full 14-puzzle benchmark
Apples-to-apples baseline: last week's qwen/qwen3.6-35b scores were recomputed on these exact same puzzles so the comparison is fair

Per-model request shaping: only Qwen models accept chat_template_kwargs.enable_thinking, so that flag is sent only to them; Gemma gets a plain request. Text-only models (gpt-oss, nemotron) were excluded — they can't process the puzzle images
This preliminary pass ran no-thinking only to stay time-boxed; the thinking comparison is the immediate next step
Scored at the individual-cell level against ground truth, same as Weeks 3–4

sections.heading: Interpretation
sections.body:
Across every model that parsed cleanly, the same shape recurs: JSON structure comes back perfect while color values are the weak point — and a model from a different family (Gemma) behaves just like the Qwen models. That is strong evidence the color-perception bottleneck is a general property of current vLLM vision models on this task, not a quirk of one Qwen build.
The practical takeaway: the fix is unlikely to be "pick a better model" — the new models don't beat the Week 4 baseline. It points back at the representation — making colors easier to read (legends, explicit cell labels) — which is exactly where the Week 4 legend win came from.

sections.heading: Next Steps
items: Run the deferred thinking comparison for the two Qwen models on this subset, then scale the strongest models up to all 14 puzzles for a real head-to-head
Push the representation fixes (explicit integer labels on cells, higher-contrast swatches) now that the bottleneck is confirmed cross-model
Treat qwen3-vl:32b's parse failures as an infra finding (Ollama vs vLLM backend), not a capability result, when choosing models going forward

title: The Timeout That Wasn't (and Does Thinking Help?)
excerpt: A wave of “timeout” errors against the cluster turned out to be something else entirely. Fixing it rebuilt the request pipeline, uncovered a useful fact about streaming, and finally let the legend-and-thinking comparison run. The legend helped color accuracy; chain-of-thought, surprisingly, didn’t.

sections.heading: Overview
sections.body: Week 3 established that the vision model reconstructs MARC puzzle structure flawlessly but reads colors only about half the time. The plan for this stretch was a direct follow-up: add a color legend to the rendered images and switch on the model’s thinking mode, then measure whether either lifts color accuracy. Instead, most of the time went to a debugging detour — a wave of “timeout” errors from the MindRouter cluster that, on inspection, weren’t timeouts at all. Chasing that down rebuilt the whole request pipeline and surfaced a genuinely useful fact about how the cluster behaves. With the pipeline fixed, the legend-and-thinking comparison finally ran end to end.

sections.heading: The “Timeout” That Wasn’t
sections.body:
The symptom: the reconstruction run kept failing against a fast H200 cluster that had no business being slow. The thinking-mode run failed 13 of 14 puzzles; the no-thinking run dropped its 2 heaviest. The errors looked like timeouts, but the saved responses told a different story — every failure was an HTTP 404, and the failures scaled precisely with output length, not cluster load.
The chain: our requests were non-streaming with huge output budgets, so MindRouter had to buffer the entire multi-thousand-token response from the backend. That buffering overran the cluster’s 180s-per-attempt / 300s-total backend timeout, so MindRouter cancelled the generation. Repeated cancellations tripped each backend’s circuit breaker, and once every backend serving the model was tripped, the scheduler had no healthy backend left — so it returned 404, not a timeout. Our own retry logic then made it worse by retrying those 404s with exponential backoff, turning each failure into a multi-minute hang.
The lesson: a powerful GPU cluster raises throughput, not single-stream latency. Generating tens of thousands of tokens one at a time is inherently sequential, and no amount of cluster horsepower beats a 300-second buffer window.

sections.heading: What We Changed
items: Streaming: switched every reconstruction request to server-sent events, accumulating the answer and the reasoning trace as separate deltas, so the connection stays alive through a long generation instead of buffering it all at once

Retry policy: stopped retrying 404s (a client-side error per MindRouter’s own docs), stopped re-running expensive non-idempotent POSTs on a read timeout, and now surface MindRouter’s error body instead of a bare status code
Pacing: added a short delay between puzzles plus a circuit-breaker cooldown after any failure, so a tripped backend has time to recover instead of cascading into the next request
Budgets: right-sized the output token caps per mode rather than sending one oversized request that could never finish in time

sections.heading: A Useful Discovery: Streaming Has No 300-Second Ceiling
sections.body:
We had assumed the documented 300-second cap was a hard wall for every request. It isn’t. A deliberate probe — a streaming request with an absurd 60,000-token budget meant to force a server-side cutoff — instead ran for 532 seconds (nearly 9 minutes) and finished cleanly, stopping only when it hit the token cap. The 300s timeout governs how long MindRouter waits for a buffered (non-streaming) response; once a stream is flowing, the request rides along as long as tokens keep arriving. This is exactly why switching to streaming didn’t just reduce the timeouts — it removed that failure mode entirely.
532sLongest clean stream
60,000Tokens, no cutoff
113/sDecode rate
1.7sTime to first token

sections.heading: Results: The Legend Helps, Thinking Doesn’t
sections.body:
With the pipeline fixed, the actual experiment ran. Adding a color legend to the images — a swatch mapping each integer to its color — lifted no-thinking cell accuracy from Week 3’s 50.4% (no legend) to 62.1% (legend) across the same 6,912 cells. That’s a clear, cheap win.

Thinking mode was the surprise. It parsed only 9 of 14 puzzles (more on the other 5 below), and even on the 9 it did answer, it gave no overall benefit: 57.5% cell accuracy versus no-thinking’s 59.5% on the exact same puzzles. Per-puzzle it was a high-variance coin flip — chain-of-thought helped a few and badly hurt others.

sections.heading: The Reasoning-Runaway Problem
sections.body:
Why did thinking mode fail to answer 5 puzzles outright? Not a timeout, not a crash — the model simply never stopped reasoning. On dense puzzles it narrates the grids cell-by-cell in its chain-of-thought (“row 4 col 6 is light blue, row 4 col 7 is green…”), burning its entire token budget on transcription before it ever emits the JSON answer. The reasoning trace runs to 20,000–30,000 tokens and gets cut off mid-sentence, leaving the answer field empty.
Puzzle (no JSON produced)Reasoning at cutoff
traffic_has_rules_follow_them~30,200 tokens
green_means_go…traffic_jams~23,700 tokens
debris_protects_little_fish~22,200 tokens
fish_that_see_the_fisherman…~21,600 tokens
using_your_blush…depletes_it~21,400 tokens

We tried to rein it in — prompts forbidding cell-by-cell transcription, an explicit “two short paragraphs then answer” limit, and a small temperature bump to break repetition loops. These rescued most puzzles, but a stubborn handful ignore every brevity instruction and run away regardless. Low-effort reasoning is not something this model can be reliably forced into for dense grids.

sections.heading: Interpretation
sections.body:
The color legend is a clean win: cheap to add, ~12 points of cell accuracy, no downside. Naive chain-of-thought is not — it doesn’t improve color perception on the puzzles it answers, and it actively risks producing nothing at all on the dense ones, where the model spends its whole budget describing cells instead of committing to an answer.
The throughline from Week 3 holds: the bottleneck is perception, not reasoning. Giving the model more room to think doesn’t help it see colors it was already misreading — it just gives it more room to second-guess. The reference signal (the legend) helps; the deliberation (thinking) doesn’t.

sections.heading: Next Steps
items: Make the thinking comparison complete by taming the runaway puzzles — likely a two-pass “reason, then answer in a separate call” structure so reasoning length can’t starve the answer
Push the legend idea further: explicit integer labels printed on each cell, or larger / higher-contrast swatches, to attack the color-disambiguation bottleneck head-on
Probe which color pairs the model confuses most, using the per-cell diff data already in the visual reports
Begin the core MARC question now that the pipeline is solid: does the metaphor clue improve puzzle-solving accuracy over a no-metaphor baseline?

title: Can a VLLM Read a MARC Puzzle?
excerpt: Benchmarked a vision LLM on pure image-to-JSON reconstruction of all 14 MARC puzzles. The model nailed the structure every time — but color accuracy tells a more complicated story.

sections.heading: Overview
sections.body: This week's core question: if you hand a vision LLM nothing but a rendered MARC puzzle image, can it reconstruct the original JSON representation? This is a foundational sanity check — the MARC pipeline assumes models can accurately perceive grid structure and color values from visual input. A perfect reconstruction score would mean the image encoding is lossless from the model's perspective. The results were more nuanced than expected.

sections.heading: Methodology
items: Generated PNG images for all 14 MARC puzzles using the existing generate_images.py renderer (training pairs fully visible; test outputs hidden as ?)
Sent each image to qwen/qwen3.6-35b on the MindRouter H200 cluster via the OpenAI-compatible /v1/chat/completions endpoint — image only, no JSON source data
Prompted the model to output a strict JSON object matching the puzzle format: metaphor string, train pairs (input + output grids), and test input
Disabled thinking mode via "chat_template_kwargs": {"enable_thinking": false} and enforced JSON output with "response_format": {"type": "json_object"}
Compared model output against ground-truth JSON at the individual cell level, normalizing for string vs. integer encoding

sections.body:

The model successfully produced valid, structurally correct JSON for every single puzzle. Grid dimensions, nesting, and field names were always right. But cell-level value accuracy was only ~50% — essentially the model is reliably reading where things are, but frequently misidentifying what color they are.

sections.heading: Interpretation
sections.body:
The model can read puzzle structure perfectly — it never hallucinates extra grids, gets the dimensions wrong, or drops fields. The problem is color disambiguation: the 10-color ARC palette contains several visually similar hues that the model conflates.
Two patterns stand out in the per-puzzle breakdown. Puzzles with fewer distinct colors and high contrast (e.g., light_illuminates_walls_and_shadows_form at 71%) do much better. Puzzles that use many similar colors or have dense, repetitive patterns (e.g., vote_according_to_your_party at just 17%) collapse almost entirely. This strongly suggests the bottleneck is color perception, not structural understanding.

sections.heading: Infrastructure Findings
items: vLLM vs Ollama throughput: Initial tests used qwen3-vl:32b (Ollama backend), which caused 502 gateway errors and 20+ minute hangs per request. Switching to qwen/qwen3.6-35b (vLLM backend) resolved this entirely — all 14 puzzles completed in minutes via continuous batching on the H200 cluster

Thinking mode: The /no_think prompt suffix is not the correct API approach. MindRouter requires "chat_template_kwargs": {"enable_thinking": false} in the request body to properly suppress chain-of-thought for Qwen models
JSON enforcement: Setting "response_format": {"type": "json_object"} gave 14/14 parse success vs intermittent failures without it

sections.heading: Next Steps
items: Run the same benchmark with thinking enabled to test whether reasoning improves color accuracy — this is the direct comparison needed before drawing conclusions
Investigate adding a color legend to the rendered puzzle images (a swatch showing which integer maps to which color) to give the model an explicit reference
Consider testing with the ARC color names as text labels on the grid cells rather than relying on visual color alone
Begin the main MARC experiment: does the metaphor clue improve puzzle-solving accuracy over no-metaphor baseline?
